addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. - general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- graphify: Use for any question about a codebase, its architecture, file relationships, or project content — especially when graphify-out/ exists, where the question should be treated as a graphify query first. Turns any input (code, docs, papers, images, videos) into a persistent knowledge graph with god nodes, community detection, and query/path/explain tools.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

input.description: Find webhook delivery and SSRF protection
input.prompt:
Search this repository very thoroughly for:

1. A webhook or notification delivery system that sends outbound HTTP requests when content changes. I need the specific function that actually executes/sends the HTTP request outbound.

2. An SSRF protection mechanism — something that validates/checks URLs to prevent requests to internal/private network addresses (e.g., checking for localhost, private IP ranges like 10.x, 192.168.x, 127.x, etc.).

Search breadth: very thorough. Look for terms like: webhook, deliver, notify, outbound, SSRF, ssrf_filter, url_validator, private_ip, internal_address, reserved_ip, localhost check, ip_filter, address validation, forbid_local, network_guard, etc. Check in all languages and frameworks present.

Report the exact file paths and function/method names for both.

content.text:
Here are the complete findings:

---

## 1. Webhook / Notification Delivery System -- Outbound HTTP Request Function

**File:** `/bench/home/work/internal/webhook/webhook.go`

**Function:** `Post` (line 120)

This is the function that actually constructs and sends the outbound HTTP POST request to webhook endpoints. It:
- Marshals the `WebhookRequestPayload` to JSON
- Creates an `http.NewRequest("POST", ...)` to the target URL
- Optionally signs the request using HMAC-SHA256 (Standard Webhooks spec) if a `SigningSecret` is set, adding `webhook-id`, `webhook-timestamp`, and `webhook-signature` headers
- Executes the request via `safeClient.Do(req)` (line 152), where `safeClient` is an `*http.Client` configured with SSRF-safe transport
- Reads and validates the response

There is also an async variant:

**Function:** `PostAsync` (line 184) -- enqueues the payload into a buffered channel (`asyncPostQueue`, capacity 128) for background dispatch by one of 4 goroutine workers (initialized in `init()`, line 42). Each worker calls `Post()`.

The callers that trigger webhook dispatch on content changes are in:

**File:** `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/memo_service_webhooks.go`

- `(*APIV1Service).DispatchMemoCreatedWebhook` (line 15)
- `(*APIV1Service).DispatchMemoUpdatedWebhook` (line 19)
- `(*APIV1Service).DispatchMemoDeletedWebhook` (line 23)
- `(*APIV1Service).DispatchMemoCommentCreatedWebhook` (line 30)

All of these retrieve the user's configured webhooks from the store, build a `WebhookRequestPayload`, and call `webhook.PostAsync(payload)`.

---

## 2. SSRF Protection Mechanism

**File:** `/bench/home/work/internal/webhook/validate.go`

This file contains the URL and IP validation logic:

**Function:** `isReservedIP` (line 44) -- checks whether a given `net.IP` falls within any reserved/private CIDR range. The blocked ranges (defined in `reservedCIDRs`, line 14) are:
- `127.0.0.0/8` (IPv4 loopback)
- `10.0.0.0/8` (RFC-1918 class A)
- `172.16.0.0/12` (RFC-1918 class B)
- `192.168.0.0/16` (RFC-1918 class C)
- `169.254.0.0/16` (link-local, including cloud IMDS at 169.254.169.254)
- `::1/128` (IPv6 loopback)
- `fc00::/7` (IPv6 unique local)
- `fe80::/10` (IPv6 link-local)

There is a global toggle `AllowPrivateIPs` (line 41) that disables the SSRF check when set to `true` (for self-hosted deployments targeting local-network services).

**Function:** `ValidateURL` (line 62) -- the registration-time check. Called when a user creates or updates a webhook (see `CreateUserWebhook` and `UpdateUserWebhook` in `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/user_service_webhooks.go`). It:
1. Parses the raw URL
2. Enforces `http` or `https` scheme only
3. Resolves the hostname via `net.LookupHost`
4. Calls `isReservedIP` on every resolved IP, rejecting the URL if any falls in a private range

**File:** `/bench/home/work/internal/webhook/webhook.go`

**Function:** `safeDialContext` (line 59) -- the runtime/dial-time SSRF guard. This is wired into the `http.Transport` of the `safeClient` (line 34) so it runs at the moment the TCP connection is established, defeating DNS rebinding attacks. It:
1. Splits the address into host and port
2. Resolves the hostname via `net.DefaultResolver.LookupHost`
3. Calls `isReservedIP` on every resolved IP, refusing to connect if any is private/reserved
4. Only if all IPs pass does it proceed with the actual `net.Dialer.DialContext`

This two-layer design (validate at registration time in `ValidateURL`, and again at dial time in `safeDialContext`) ensures SSRF protection cannot be bypassed by DNS rebinding -- where a hostname resolves to a public IP at registration but a private IP at request time.

h02.

The outbound webhook delivery executes in the `Post` function in `internal/webhook/webhook.go` (with `PostAsync` enqueuing work to background goroutines that call `Post`). The actual HTTP call goes through a `safeClient` whose transport uses `safeDialContext` (same file), which resolves the target hostname at dial time and checks every resolved IP against a blocklist of reserved/private CIDR ranges defined in `internal/webhook/validate.go`.

**Delivery function** — `Post` in `internal/webhook/webhook.go`; **protection mechanism** — SSRF guard via `isReservedIP` / `safeDialContext` in `internal/webhook/webhook.go` and `ValidateURL` in `internal/webhook/validate.go`. The protection is two-layered: `ValidateURL` (`validate.go`) rejects private-IP targets at webhook registration time, and `safeDialContext` (`webhook.go`) re-checks at TCP dial time to defeat DNS rebinding.
